newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: FEATURE - Czechs still wrestling with communist-era crimes.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Czechs still wrestling with communist-era crimes.

text.p: The trial of Jaroslav Daniel, known as "The Pig" by his victims, touched a national nerve in the Czech Republic and rekindled the debate over the retribution for communist-era crimes.
Daniel was jailed for five years in April for abuse of power and causing serious bodily harm.

During his trial Daniel laughed when his victims described how the communist interrogator had flayed the soles of their feet with cable and dispensed beatings so brutal they were still suffering the effects four decades later.
Daniel's case could be one of the easier ones facing prosecutors who are treading a legal minefield to try to bring to book the perpetrators of four decades of communist rule.

His trial could be just the first of many this year, which the Office for the Documentation and Investigation of the Crimes of Communism (UDV) has described as a watershed in Czech efforts to bring former communists into the dock.
"It is a problem which is extremely important for society and we won't solve it simply by waving a magic wand," said UDV chief Vaclav Benda, a former dissident.
TREASON CHARGES DATING BACK TO 1968

The most serious cases concern three former politburo members accused of treason in connection with the 1968 Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia. They are Milos Jakes, Communist Party chief overthrown during the 1989 "Velvet Revolution", one-time prime minister Jozef Lenart and Karel Hoffmann, a former central committee member.
The affair is complicated by the fact that the defendants are accused of betraying a state which no longer exists -- the Czechoslovak Socialist Republic.

The chances of a successful prosecution are far from clear and a number of similar charges drawn up by the UDV against other former communist leaders were dropped by state lawyers for lack of evidence.

Only one top communist, Prague party leader Miroslav Stepan, has served a jail sentence since 1989. He was jailed for four years in July 1990 for "abuse of power" but paroled later on appeal. The other 20 or so cases expected to come to trial this year concern former policemen, StB secret police interrogators like Daniel, and border guards facing charges of murder, torture and illegal imprisonment.

"It is hard to catch the big fish. On the one hand, some are already dead, and on the other hand, they did not carry out brutal violence," says Jan Pospisil, a lawyer at the UDV who spent 10 years in communist jails.
"It is difficult to prove that some deputy minister ordered it, and there are even cases where they ordered the opposite -- although, of course, that was just camouflage."
PROCESS MIRED IN POLITICAL DISPUTE
The proposed trials have run into opposition.

The Communist Party of Bohemia and Moravia (KSCM), which came third in last year's elections with 10 percent of the vote and is more pro-reform than the old hardliners, has attacked the whole process as politically motivated.
And the mainstream opposition party, the Social Democrats, accuses the centre-right government of not being seriously interested in settling accounts with the past.
"It's good these cases are taking place, but it is too late," says Social Democrat shadow interior minister Jaroslav Basta.
"This government had reservations about punishing members of the nomenklatura (political establishment) from the second half of the 1980s and was often in some way linked with them," he says.

"After 1989, dissidents filed loads of charges and for several years they were successfully shunted around from office to office: at one time, the Office for the Protection of Democracy was investigating them, then it was the Interior Ministry's inspection department, now it is the UDV."
But these are arguments that Benda has little time for. "If the government did not want to deal with this question, this office would never have been set up," he said.
"Of course the priorities were different -- they had to be. We had to build a democratic society, a state based on the rule of law, a prospering economy."
STRICT LEGAL APPROACH MEETS OTHER OBSTACLES
Aside from these arguments, there are a number of generally accepted reasons for the lack of success in bringing former communists to trial.

In the immediate aftermath of the "Velvet Revolution", there was a lack of experienced lawyers not connected with the communists. As late as May this year, a state attorney resigned when it was alleged that he had instigated repression in the 1980s.
Further delay was caused by the 1993 break-up of Czechoslovakia, which diverted attention from the problem and also brought legal complications.
Benda says this kind of thing was only to be expected. "It is precisely because we want to proceed very strictly that this is not revolutionary revenge but a quite correct legal approach," he said.
But Basta said the apparent lack of action could have dire consequences.

"Yet again, we are convincing people that justice does not exist. This is dangerous because, if you look at Czech history, you find people were taught for 60 years that it pays not to be decent, that it pays to collaborate with any regime at all, and that nothing will happen to anyone afterwards anyway."
